2.1 Internal model stability proofThe internal model of the EMC unit can be formulated in the form of state equations as follows, [3]
\[x(k + 1) = \begin{bmatrix} x_c \\ x_d \end{bmatrix} (k + 1) = \begin{bmatrix} A_c & H_c \\ 0 & A_d \end{bmatrix} x(k) + \begin{bmatrix} y_m \end{bmatrix}\]

where \(x_c\) and \(x_d\) refer to the controllable (or canonical) and rejector states, respectively.

On the other side, the matrices \(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}\), are related respectively to: (i) the state \(\mathbf{x},\) (ii) the control input \(\mathbf{u}\), and (iii) the estimated output from the internal model \(\mathbf{y}_m\). In addition the matrix \(\mathbf{G}\) is present, for the estimation of the noise vector \(\bar{\mathbf{w}}\). In particular, the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is made by the sub-matrices: \(\mathbf{A}_c\), related to \(\mathbf{x}_c\), \(\mathbf{A}_d\) related to \(\mathbf{x}_d\), and \(\mathbf{H}_c\), which considers the interactions of \(\mathbf{x}_d\) on \(\mathbf{x}_c\). Similarly, we have the sub-matrices \(\mathbf{B}_c\) and \(\mathbf{B}_d\) for \(\mathbf{B}\) matrix, \(\mathbf{G}_c\) and \(\mathbf{G}_d\) for \(\mathbf{G}\) matrix, \(\mathbf{C}_c\) and \(\mathbf{C}_d\) for \(\mathbf{C}\) matrix.

Equation (1) for the internal model can be converted from time to frequency domain, as follows
\[\mathbf{X}(z) = \{z\mathbb{I} - [\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{GLC}]\}^{-1} \mathbf{X}(0) + \frac{\mathbf{X}_{s_i}(z)}{k + 1} \mathbf{X}_{s_i}(z) + \mathbf{B} \{z\mathbb{I} - [\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{GLC}]\}^{-1} \mathbf{U}(z) + \frac{\mathbf{Y}_{m}(z)}{k + 1} \mathbf{Y}_{m}(z) + \mathbf{G} \{z\mathbb{I} - [\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{GLC}]\}^{-1} \mathbf{Y}(z)\]

where \(\mathbf{X}_{s(i)}(z)\) denotes the zero-input response of the closed-loop system when \(\mathbf{U}(z) = \mathbf{Y}(z) = 0\), \(\mathbf{X}_{s,N}(z)\) the zero state response when \(\mathbf{X}(0) = \mathbf{Y}(z) = 0\) and \(\mathbf{X}_{s,0}(z)\) the zero state response when \(\mathbf{X}(0) = \mathbf{U}(z) = 0\).

Both the internal and BIBO stability of the internal model can be studied by imposing \(\det\{z\mathbb{I} - [\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{GLC}]\}^{-1}\) equal to a characteristic polynomial (\(z - p_1)(z - p_2) ... (z - p_n)\), where \(n\) is the \(\mathbf{A}\) matrix dimension: in order to guarantee the asymptotic stability, the poles \([p_1, p_2, ..., p_n]\) must lie inside the unitary circle. From the equation above it is clear that the stability finally depends on the observer matrix \(\mathbf{L}\) components’ design, which will be discussed in Section 2.5.

2.2 Plant stability proofThe plant of the DC motor, i.e. the mathematical description of the DC motor physical behaviour, must guarantee BIBO stability. Equation (3) define the state equations for the DC motor
\[\begin{cases} \omega(k + 1) = \left(\frac{1}{\tau_m} T_s + 1 \right) \omega(k) + \frac{T_s}{\tau_{m}k_v} V_a(k) + d(k), \\ x_d(1 + k) = (T_s + 1)x_d(1) + T_s[x_d(2) + \overline{w}(2)], \\ x_d(2 + k) = (T_s + 1)x_d(2) + T_s \overline{w}(3)(k), \end{cases}\]d(k) = \(T_s[\overline{w}(1) + x_d(1)](k)], \omega(0) = \omega_0, x_d(0) = x_d10, x_d(2)(k) = x_d20,

 (3)

where \(\omega\) is the DC motor output speed, \(\tau_m\) is the DC motor mechanical time constant, \(k_v\) is the back electromotive force constant specifically found for the studied motor, \([\overline{w}_1, \overline{w}_2, \overline{w}_3]\) are the components of the noise vector \(\overline{w}\), \([x_d1, x_d2]\) are the components of the disturbance state \(\mathbf{x}_{d}\), \(T_{s}\) is the sampling time.

Equation (3) can be translated in frequency domain and reshaped in a matrix form, i.e.
\[W_M(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{U(z)} = \frac{\beta_0(z+1)}{z^2 + \alpha_1 z + \alpha_0},\] \[\beta_0 = \frac{T^2}{k_v(\tau_m T + 2 \tau_m \tau_a)},\] \[\alpha_0 = \frac{T^2 - \tau_m T + 2 \tau_m \tau_a}{\tau_m T+ 2 \tau_m \tau_a},\] \[\alpha_1 = \frac{T^2 - 4 \tau_m \tau_a}{\tau_m T + 2 \tau_m \tau_a}\]

The worst case for the stability corresponds to the lowest sampling time possible. For example, by considering for \(T_{s}\) a range of \([0.01, 0.03] s\), the lowest sampling time corresponds to \(T_{s} = 0.01 s\): hence the

### 2.3 Reference dynamics stability proof

The reference dynamics equations are recalled from [1]

\[\begin{aligned}
&\bar{x}(k+1) = A_x\bar{x}(k)+B_x\bar{r}(k), \\
&\bar{v}(k) = C_x\bar{x}(k), \\
&A_R = A_c - B_cK_R, \\
&B_R = B_cN_R, \quad C_R = C_c.
\end{aligned} \tag{6}\]

The reference trajectory \(\bar{r}(k)\) is obtained by exploiting a static-state feedback, with as nominal control input \(\bar{u}(k) = -\textbf{K}_R\bar{x}(k) + \textbf{N}_R\bar{r}(k)\), where \(\textbf{K}_R = k_R\) and \(\textbf{N}_R = n_R\) are the reference generator gains.

The reference dynamics internal and BIBO stability can be studied by exploiting (6) into frequency domain:

\[\frac{\bar{x}(z) - z\left[z\bar{z} - \bar{A}_R\right]^{-1}\bar{x}(0) + B_R\left(z\bar{z} - \bar{A}_R\right)^{-1}\bar{r}(z)}{\bar{x}_{zi}(z)} = \frac{K_{rtrl}(z)}{\bar{x}_{zsi}(z)} \tag{7}\]

where \(\bar{x}_{zi}(z)\) denotes the zero-input response (hence when \(\textbf{R}(z) = 0\)), \(\bar{x}_{zs}(z)\) the zero state response when \(\textbf{X}(0) = 0\), \(\bar{R}\) the reference trajectory input \(\bar{r}\) translated in frequency domain. The stability depends on the term \([z\bar{z}-\bar{A}_R]^{-1}\). Indeed, by applying the pole-placement technique, the continuous-time eigenvalue \(\bar{A}_R = a_R\) is user-defined to lie in the right-half plane, to guarantee stability in frequency-domain. 

### 2.4 Control law stability proof

The controller block is part of an external closed-loop system, including a PI controller and the internal model controllable dynamics.

The EMC control law is made up by three terms: (i) the feed-forward component \(\bar{u}\), (ii) the state feedback \(\textbf{u}_{trk} = \textbf{K}_c\bar{e}\), and (iii) the disturbance rejection term \(\textbf{u}_d = \textbf{M} \textit{x}_d\). Ergo, being \(\bar{e}\) the tracking error, the full command expression holds:

\[\begin{aligned}
& \textbf{u}(k) = \bar{u}(k) + K_c\bar{e}(k) - \textbf{M}x_d(k), \\
&\bar{e}(k) = (\bar{x}(k) - \textit{Q} x_d(k)) - x_c(k).
\end{aligned} \tag{8}\]

The control block state equations are defined as follows, [1]

\[\begin{aligned}
 \pdiff{t}{\textbf{x}_1(k+1)} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \pdiff{\textbf{x}_1}{\textbf{x}_2(k+1)} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \pdiff{\textbf{x}_2}{\textbf{x}_3(k+1)} & \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \\
 \bar{A}_{ctrl} &= \begin{bmatrix} -A_c-k_pB_c & k_iB_c \\ -1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \\
 \bar{x}_{zsi(k)} &= \begin{bmatrix} k_pB_c \\ \end{bmatrix}, \\
 \bar{A}_c &= -\frac{Ts}{T_m}+1, \quad \bar{B}_c = \frac{Ts}{T_mk_i/M}
\end{aligned} \tag{9}\]

where \(\textbf{x}_1 = \textbf{x}_c\) is the already defined controllable state of the internal model and \(\textbf{x}_2\) is the augmented state introduced by the PI controller.

Both the internal and BIBO stability can be studied following (9), translated in frequency domain:

\[\begin{aligned}
\&\frac{G_{ctrl}(z)}{\bar{X}_{ctrl}(z) = z\left[z\bar{z} - \bar{A}_ctrl\right]^{-1}\bar{x}_{ctrl}(0) + G_{syn}(z)}{\bar{X}_{ctrl,z}(z)} \\
&\quad + \frac{G_{ctrl}(z)[\bar{z} - \bar{A}_{ctrl}]^{-1}\bar{e}(z)}{\bar{x}_{ctrl,z}(z)}
\end{aligned} \tag{10}\]

where \(\bar{X}_{ctrl, zi}(z)\) denotes the zero-input response (hence when the tracking error \(\bar{e}(z) = 0\)), \(\bar{X}_{ctrl,zs}(z)\) the zero state response when \(\bar{X}_{ctrl}(0) = 0\). Similarly as before, the stability analysis depends on the term \([z\bar{z}-\bar{A}_{ctrl}]^{-1}\), which can be solved by applying the pole-placement technique.

### 2.5 Noise estimator stability proof

The noise estimator block goal is to achieve the closed-loop stabilization of the predictor as well as to ensure a suitable disturbance estimation capability, i.e. estimate the noise vector $\overline{w}$. The noise estimator block governing equations are as follows

$$\overline{w}(k) = \begin{bmatrix} \overline{w}_1 \\ \overline{w}_2 \\ \overline{w}_3 \end{bmatrix} (k) = L_e m(k) = \begin{bmatrix} l_1 \\ l_2 \\ l_3 \end{bmatrix} e_{m}(k),$$

$$e_{m}(k) = y(k) - y_m(k).$$ (11)

In (11), $y_m$ is the estimated output of the internal model, $y$ is the measurement output of the plant, while $L$ collects the closed-loop predictor gains $l_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, 3$, for the specific DC motor case. As a result, the closed-loop predictor model can be determined by designing and tuning the $l_k$ gains trading-off between the closed-loop stability and the estimation performance.

A static-feedback is selected for the design of noise estimator, and its stability analysis is already studied in [1], Appendix B.

### 2.6 Asynchronous sampling time stability remarks

From the experimental design perspective, the discrete-time eigenvalues of the control unit naturally change at each time-step. This is directly related to the nature of the NCS environment, characterised by highly variable sampling times. As a result, the adopted design solution was based on the design of a set of continuous-time eigenvalues first, focusing on expected stability and performance level. In particular, $\mu_k$ are the control law continuous-time eigenvalues, $\mu_R$ the reference dynamics eigenvalues and finally $\mu_N$ the predictor eigenvalues. Indeed, such a continuous-time set of eigenvalues, $\mu_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, do not depend on the variable sampling time and can be then converted, at every time-step, into discrete-time eigenvalues $\lambda_i = e^{\mu_i T_{s,k}}$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, being $T_{s,k}$ the generic sampling time of the $k^{th}$ time-step.

In Figure 1 the discrete-time domain eigenvalues are presented, for reference dynamics $\lambda_R = e^{\mu_R T_s}$, control law $\lambda_K = e^{\mu_K T_s}$ and predictor $\lambda_N = e^{\mu_N T_s}$; it can be seen that, for the defined variation of $T_s$, spanning from 0.01s to 0.03s, the values are always inside the unitary circle, thus guaranteeing asymptotic stability.

![Figure 1](Figure 1: Experimental results: polar plot of the stability conditions of the control system, for $T_s = [0.01, 0.03]$ s)

**4** **Conclusion**

This work is intended to give additional studies and results to the main work _Embedded Model Control of Networked Control Systems: an Experimental Case- study_, [1]. In this main work, the Embedded Model Control (EMC) methodology is applied to design a complete digital control unit for a differential-drive mobile robot controlled in a network controlled system (NCS), thus operating in a scenario characterised by a varying sampling time and asynchronous command execution.

At the beginning, this complementary paper presents a study on the stability analysis of the EMC, in the case of the differential-drive robot setup; namely the setup explored in [1]. Furthermore, experimental tests are added to those presented in [1].

The first test verified the EMC asynchronous timing disturbance rejection capabilities, in the case of the differential-drive robot setup. The second experiment aimed to test the EMC in critical asynchronous NCS scenarios, with high delays of the timestamp. The EMC resulted to have satisfactory control behaviours until high ranges of variable timestamp, thus validating the high practical applicability of the EMC control. Another experiment benchmarked the proposed EMC asynchronous architecture with a Proportional-Integral controller (a design showing a more satisfactory control behaviour than other control architectures, e.g. PID). The experimental benchmarking study showed that the EMC has a better tracking performance than the PI controller, thanks to the presence of the new disturbance rejection control
